name: Cervical Facet Joint Syndrome
description: Facet-mediated cervical pain provoked by extension and ipsilateral rotation. Mechanical loading, postural strain or overuse can sensitise nociceptors locally and drive movement-evoked pain in the cervical spine and surrounding cervicoscapular musculature. Patients typically describe pain provoked by characteristic positions or activities, with reproducible findings on physical examination of the cervical spine and surrounding cervicoscapular musculature. Management is phase-based — protect and modulate symptoms early, then restore mobility, motor control and graded loading, progressing to functional and sport- or work-specific demands.
key_findings: Clinical findings consistent with cervical facet joint syndrome on history and physical examination.
diagnostic_tips: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging only when red flags are present or if it will change management.

treatment_plan.acute: Protect tissue; modulate pain (manual therapy, modalities as adjunct); patient education on load management.
treatment_plan.subacute: Restore ROM and motor control; introduce graded isometric/isotonic loading specific to involved tissue.
treatment_plan.chronic: Progressive resistance, capacity building and functional/sport-specific loading aligned with patient goals.

etiology: Multifactorial: load, capacity and individual risk factors interact in Cervical Facet Joint Syndrome.
epidemiology: Cervical musculoskeletal presentation commonly seen in physiotherapy practice.
pathophysiology: Tissue-specific (e.g., tendinopathy continuum, OA process, nerve compression model).
clinical_presentation: Facet-mediated cervical pain provoked by extension and ipsilateral rotation.
imaging: Plain radiograph if indicated
MRI/US for soft-tissue characterization when needed
prognosis: Generally favourable with appropriate, progressive rehabilitation.
return_to_activity: Criterion-based: pain control, ROM, strength symmetry and functional performance.

Neural tissue irritation, compression or sensitisation along the relevant peripheral or central pathway can produce radicular, referred or dermatomal symptoms. Patients typically describe pain provoked by characteristic positions or activities, with reproducible findings on physical examination of the glenohumeral joint, rotator cuff and scapulothoracic complex. Management is phase-based — protect and modulate symptoms early, then restore mobility, motor control and graded loading, progressing to functional and sport- or work-specific demands.
key_findings: Clinical findings consistent with parsonage–turner syndrome on history and physical examination.
diagnostic_tips: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging only when red flags are present or if it will change management.

treatment_plan.acute: Protect tissue; modulate pain (manual therapy, modalities as adjunct); patient education on load management.
treatment_plan.subacute: Restore ROM and motor control; introduce graded isometric/isotonic loading specific to involved tissue.
treatment_plan.chronic: Progressive resistance, capacity building and functional/sport-specific loading aligned with patient goals.

Tissue healing constraints, surgical approach and protective phase precautions strongly dictate the rehab progression and load tolerance. Patients typically describe pain provoked by characteristic positions or activities, with reproducible findings on physical examination of the hip joint, gluteal complex and surrounding myofascial structures. Management is phase-based — protect and modulate symptoms early, then restore mobility, motor control and graded loading, progressing to functional and sport- or work-specific demands.
key_findings: Clinical findings consistent with post total hip arthroplasty (posterior approach) on history and physical examination.
diagnostic_tips: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging only when red flags are present or if it will change management.

treatment_plan.acute: Protect tissue; modulate pain (manual therapy, modalities as adjunct); patient education on load management.
treatment_plan.subacute: Restore ROM and motor control; introduce graded isometric/isotonic loading specific to involved tissue.
treatment_plan.chronic: Progressive resistance, capacity building and functional/sport-specific loading aligned with patient goals.

etiology: Multifactorial: load, capacity and individual risk factors interact in Post Total Hip Arthroplasty (Posterior Approach).
epidemiology: Hip post-surgical presentation commonly seen in physiotherapy practice.
pathophysiology: Tissue-specific (e.g., tendinopathy continuum, OA process, nerve compression model).
clinical_presentation: Posterior-approach THA rehabilitation with precautions.
imaging: Plain radiograph if indicated

prognosis: Generally favourable with appropriate, progressive rehabilitation.
return_to_activity: Criterion-based: pain control, ROM, strength symmetry and functional performance.

Mechanical loading, postural strain or overuse can sensitise nociceptors locally and drive movement-evoked pain in the elbow joint, common extensor/flexor origin and forearm musculature. Patients typically describe pain provoked by characteristic positions or activities, with reproducible findings on physical examination of the elbow joint, common extensor/flexor origin and forearm musculature. Management is phase-based — protect and modulate symptoms early, then restore mobility, motor control and graded loading, progressing to functional and sport- or work-specific demands.
key_findings: Clinical findings consistent with olecranon bursitis — acute stage on history and physical examination.
diagnostic_tips: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging only when red flags are present or if it will change management.

treatment_plan.acute: Protect tissue; modulate pain (manual therapy, modalities as adjunct); patient education on load management.
treatment_plan.subacute: Restore ROM and motor control; introduce graded isometric/isotonic loading specific to involved tissue.
treatment_plan.chronic: Progressive resistance, capacity building and functional/sport-specific loading aligned with patient goals.

Neural tissue irritation, compression or sensitisation along the relevant peripheral or central pathway can produce radicular, referred or dermatomal symptoms. Patients typically describe pain provoked by characteristic positions or activities, with reproducible findings on physical examination of the wrist, carpal structures and intrinsic hand musculature. Management is phase-based — protect and modulate symptoms early, then restore mobility, motor control and graded loading, progressing to functional and sport- or work-specific demands.

diagnostic_tips: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging only when red flags are present or if it will change management.
